## The problem

`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove duplicates **in place** so that
each distinct value appears once, in the same order, packed at the front of the
array. Return `k`, the number of distinct values. Whatever sits past index
`k - 1` is ignored.

The usual example is `[0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`. After the call, the first
five slots are `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` and the return value is `5`.

A correct solution is a linear scan with a constant amount of extra memory. The
array is already sorted, so equal values come in one contiguous run.

## The plan I should have written first

This is two nested loops and two pointers, and **both pointers only move
forward**.

| Pointer | Meaning | How it moves |
|---|---|---|
| `k` | Index of the last value in the compacted unique prefix. `nums[0..k]` is the answer so far. | Increases by one only when a new distinct value is written. |
| `next` | Read index into the part of the array not yet folded into that prefix. | Increases only. It walks through the current run of duplicates, then stops on the next new value. |

The outer loop is "place the next distinct value." The inner loop is "skip the
rest of the run that matches `nums[k]`." Because a run is contiguous, skipping
it means `next` jumps ahead of `k`. The write fills **one** slot,
`nums[k + 1]`. It does not clear the gap `next` just jumped over.

So the invariant, after every write, is:

1. `nums[0..k]` holds the distinct values seen so far, in order.
2. `next` has already passed every index before it. Those cells may still hold
   old duplicates, and they must not be read again.
3. `nums[next]` is the value just copied (or `next` is off the end).

Anything that assigns `next` to a smaller index breaks (2).

## First attempt

```csharp
public class Solution {
    public int RemoveDuplicates(int[] nums) {
        if (nums == null || nums.Length == 0) {
            return 0;
        }
        int k = 0;
        int next = k + 1;
        while (k < nums.Length - 1) {
            next = k + 1;
            while (next < nums.Length && nums[next] == nums[k]) {
                next++;
            }
            if (next == nums.Length) {
                break;
            }
            nums[++k] = nums[next];
        }
        return k + 1;
    }
}
```

The damaging line is `next = k + 1` at the start of every outer iteration.
`next` is initialized to `k + 1` once already; the assignment inside the loop
pulls the read pointer back to the slot just after the write index.

## Where that line breaks the array

Take `[0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`.

The first two writes still look fine, because the cells just after `k` happen
to be duplicates of the current value:

1. `k = 0`, scan from index `1`, skip the second `0`, write `1` at index `1`.
   The array is `[0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`.
2. `k = 1`, scan from index `2`, skip the run of `1`s, write `2` at index `2`.
   The array is `[0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`.

Index `2` now holds `2`, but indices `3` and `4` still hold `1`. Those `1`s
were already passed when `next` jumped to the first `2`. The next outer
iteration then does `next = k + 1`, so `next` becomes `3`. The inner loop asks
whether `nums[3] == nums[2]`, that is `1 == 2`. It is not, so the loop does
not skip anything, and the write copies that stale `1`:

```text
nums[++k] = nums[3]    →    [0, 1, 2, 1, ...]
```

The unique prefix is no longer sorted and no longer unique. Later iterations
keep copying leftover values out of that gap. The call returns `9`, and the
array is `[0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4, 4]` instead of a prefix of length `5`.

The shorter input `[0, 0, 1, 1, 2]` fails the same way. After the prefix has
correctly become `[0, 1, 2, ...]`, the cell immediately after `k` still holds
an old `1`. Restarting there copies `1` back into the answer, and the method
returns `5`.

A short case can hide this. On `[1, 1, 2]` the only extra `1` sits in the cell
the write overwrites, so `k + 1` lands on the already-found `2` and the buggy
version returns the right answer. The reset is harmless only while `k` and
`next` stay adjacent. The inner loop exists to make them **not** adjacent, and
it leaves a stale gap whenever a run is longer than the single cell the write
fills. The reset and the inner loop contradict each other.

## Corrected solution

Drop the reset. `next` is set once, before either loop, and from then on both
pointers only increase.

```csharp
public class Solution {
    public int RemoveDuplicates(int[] nums) {
        if (nums == null || nums.Length == 0) {
            return 0;
        }
        int k = 0;
        int next = 1;
        while (k < nums.Length - 1) {
            while (next < nums.Length && nums[next] == nums[k]) {
                next++;
            }
            if (next == nums.Length) {
                break;
            }
            nums[++k] = nums[next];
        }
        return k + 1;
    }
}
```

On `[0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`, `next` moves `1 → 2 → 5 → 7 → 9` and never
returns to the gap it jumped. Each jump lands on a new value (`1`, then `2`,
`3`, `4`), and that value is written at `++k`. When `next` falls off the end,
the prefix is `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` and `k + 1` is `5`.

There is no infinite loop hiding in the nested version. After a write,
`nums[next] == nums[k]`, so the next inner loop advances `next` at least once
before it can stop on a different value.

Each index is visited a constant number of times, and the only extra memory is
the two indices: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. The `null` and empty
checks are outside the problem constraints (`nums` has at least one element);
they do not change the result on a legal input.

## The same rule, with the movement written into the loop

The version above is the plan I actually had: an inner loop that skips a whole
run. The usual editorial writes the same invariant as a single loop, where the
read pointer is the loop variable and so cannot be reassigned backward:

```csharp
public int RemoveDuplicates(int[] nums) {
    int k = 0;
    for (int next = 1; next < nums.Length; next++) {
        if (nums[next] != nums[k]) {
            nums[++k] = nums[next];
        }
    }
    return k + 1;
}
```

`next` still only moves forward, by one each iteration instead of jumping a
run. `k` still marks the end of the unique prefix and advances only on a new
value. The cells between them are unread leftovers, same as before. Putting
`next` in the `for` header makes the "only move forward" rule structural: the
reset that broke the first attempt cannot be written without fighting the loop.

## What I want to remember

The bug was not a slip in the inner `while`. It came from coding before the
plan was finished. I had two loops, but I had not committed to the rule that
both pointers only move forward, so `next = k + 1` looked like a reasonable way
to "start from the write index" on each pass. It re-enters a region the scan
has already finished.

Next time, before writing the loops, write down three lines:

1. What each pointer means.
2. Which way it is allowed to move.
3. Which slice of the array is finished and must not be read again.

If a line would move a pointer backward, or into that finished slice, it is not
part of the plan.
